# Becker et al., early-2025 AI and experienced open-source developer productivity

## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The authors run a randomized controlled trial to measure how AI tools at the February–June 2025 frontier affect the productivity of experienced open-source developers working in mature projects they know well: 16 developers with moderate AI experience complete 246 tasks, each randomly assigned to allow or disallow early-2025 AI tools; when AI is allowed, developers mostly use Cursor Pro with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet (Abstract, p. 1) [AE]. Developers forecast beforehand that AI would cut completion time by 24% and estimate afterwards that it cut it by 20%; "Surprisingly, we find that allowing AI actually increases completion time by 19%—AI tooling slowed developers down." [V] (Abstract, p. 1). Experts in economics and in machine learning predicted reductions of 39% and 38% (Abstract, p. 1) [AE].

To understand the result, they examine 21 properties of the setting and design that could a priori contribute to the slowdown, and conclude that "Although the influence of experimental artifacts cannot be entirely ruled out, the robustness of the slowdown effect across our analyses suggests it is unlikely to primarily be a function of our experimental design." [V] (Abstract, p. 1). They find evidence that 5 factors contribute, mixed, unclear or no evidence for 10, and evidence against 6 (§1, p. 2) [AR].

They bound the claim. Many of the contributing factors are specific to the setting, and "these results do not imply that current AI systems are not useful in many realistic, economically relevant settings" [V] (§1, p. 3); nor do they imply that future models will not speed up developers in this exact setting, or that better prompting, agent scaffolding or domain-specific finetuning of current systems could not yield positive speedup (§1, p. 3) [AR]. What they do say the results show is that "our results reveal a large disconnect between perceived and actual AI impact on developer productivity" [V] (§1, p. 3), and that both experts and developers drastically overestimate AI's usefulness for developer productivity, even after many hours using the tools (§4, p. 10) [AR].

## Part I: Why this study, and how it differs from prior work

### The inferential gap (§1, pp. 1–2)

Frontier AI systems show impressive capabilities on software benchmarks and in experiments on synthetic tasks, but "these lab experiments sacrifice realism for scale and efficiency" [V]: the tasks are self-contained, need little prior context, and are scored by algorithmic metrics that miss many important capabilities, so inferring real-world impact from them is hard (§1, p. 1) [AR] [BT]. Existing field experiments measure outcomes such as lines of code added or tasks completed, which AI can change without productivity increasing, since code can be more verbose but functionally equivalent and tasks can be split without the total work changing (§1, p. 1) [AR]. This study defines tasks before randomizing them: "Crucially, the tasks are defined before they are randomized" [V], which limits effects of AI unrelated to productivity (§1, p. 2, footnote 1) [AR].

### Background literature (§1.1, pp. 3–4)

- *Speedup, but on synthetic tasks.* Peng et al. and Paradis et al. find 56% and 21% speedups on coding tasks with AI assistance, and Weber et al. a 65% increase in the rate of task requirements satisfied; but these use artificial or synthetic tasks (§1.1, p. 3) [BT]. Peng et al.'s task, a basic HTTP server in JavaScript checked by test cases shown to the developers, is called unrepresentative of most software work and likely similar to much LLM training data, which may unfairly advantage AI systems (§1.1, p. 3) [AR].
- *Speedup, but with non-fixed outcome measures.* Studies of tasks found in the wild, via a natural experiment or RCTs, find 14–51% increases in output metrics (lines of code, commits, pull requests), measures not fixed in advance and open to the same verbosity and task-splitting effects (§1.1, p. 3) [BT] [AR].
- *Impressive benchmark results.* The general consensus about AI's effect on developer productivity is, the authors say, perhaps unsurprising given frontier AIs' impressive apparent capabilities on question-answering and agentic benchmark tasks (§1.1, p. 3) [AR].
- *Heterogeneous effects by experience.* Agrawal et al.'s framework treats AI as a fall in the cost of prediction; existing micro-level empirical work tends to find generative AI benefits less experienced workers more, compressing performance distributions; this motivates the focus on highly skilled open-source developers, a setting with relatively less research (§1.1, p. 3) [BT] [AR].
- *Other domains and economic impact.* Mixed results for CBRN uplift risk assessment; substantial productivity increases in some non-software domains; work on AI accelerating AI R&D, on explosive growth from AI labour substitution, and both optimistic and sceptical economic perspectives (§1.1, pp. 3–4) [BT].

The study's stated complements to that literature: models at the February–June 2025 frontier; unfiltered, live open-source tasks rather than synthetic or cherry-picked ones; a fixed outcome measure (speedup on tasks defined before randomized assignment); engineers with years of expertise in the target repositories; and rich data on time use, AI code suggestions and developers' qualitative experience (§1.1, p. 4) [AP].

Table 3 sets the study beside six earlier ones (Peng, Weber, Cui, Paradis, Gambacorta, Yeverechyahu), which report 56% faster, 65% faster, 26% output, 21% faster, 55% output and 37% output, against this study's 19% slower; this study is the only row the table marks as meeting all four criteria it lists (AI at or above GPT-4, non-synthetic tasks, experienced high-familiarity developers, fixed outcome measure) (App. B, pp. 17–18) [AE]. The text adds that other literature typically does not test systems more capable than GPT-4, and that no single prior study combines in-the-wild tasks, experienced developers and outcome measures that correspond directly to productivity and are fixed before treatment assignment (App. B, p. 17) [AR].

## Part II: Design and measurement

### Developers and repositories (§2.1, p. 4; App. G.7, pp. 45–46)

Developers are recruited from the authors' professional networks and from outreach to active contributors to large, popular GitHub repositories; they are experienced engineers (typically over a decade of experience) and regular contributors, with on average 5 years on their repository (59% of its lifetime) and 1,500 commits to it; they are paid $150/hour (§2.1, p. 4) [AE]. The repositories average 23,000 stars, 1,100,000 lines of code, 4,900 forks, 20,000 commits and 710 committers, and broadly have very high quality bars for contributions (§2.1, p. 4) [AE]. Named repositories include mito-ds/mito, stdlib-js/stdlib, ghc/ghc, haskell/cabal, flairNLP/flair, jsdom/jsdom, HypothesisWorks/hypothesis, devflowinc/trieve, scikit-learn/scikit-learn, EleutherAI/gpt-neox and huggingface/transformers; others are anonymized, and the developer table reports rounded representative values to preserve anonymity (App. G.7, pp. 45–46) [AE].

### Experimental design (§2.2, pp. 5–6)

Each developer lists real issues in their repository (bug reports, feature requests, work items), then forecasts how long each would take with and without AI; the forecasts serve as a proxy for difficulty and as each developer's anticipated per-issue speedup (§2.2, p. 5) [AE]. Issues are randomized to a condition by a simulated fair coin flip (§2.2, p. 5) [AE]. With AI allowed, developers may use any AI tools or models, or none if they expect AI not to help; with AI disallowed, no generative AI tooling may be used; LLM-based tab autocomplete such as GitHub Copilot is disallowed, while search engines stay allowed (§2.2, p. 5, footnote 6) [AE]. Developers work in their preferred order, sometimes on several issues at once, submit a pull request when satisfied, address the reviewer's changes, merge, and self-report time before and after review (§2.2, pp. 5–6) [AE]. About half the issues were tracked separately rather than formally defined on the repository; all are real work the developers wanted to contribute, all are submitted and reviewed through the repository's standard system, and developers are asked to keep issues to a maximum of two hours or split longer ones (§2.2, p. 5, footnote 4) [AE].

Developers get Cursor Pro subscriptions and live basic training (prompting Cursor to edit files in their own codebase, accepting changes, reverting to checkpoints), but are not required to use Cursor (§2.2.1, p. 6) [AE]. 93% have prior experience with tools like ChatGPT; only 44% with Cursor (§2.2.1, p. 6) [AE]. Developers work largely as normal, except that they typically record their screens, often use Cursor when AI is allowed (sometimes not their normal environment, such as neovim or PyCharm), and record details after each issue; broadly they reported not being significantly inconvenienced (§2.2.2, p. 6) [AE].

### The outcome measure and estimator (§2.3, pp. 6–7; App. D, pp. 28–31)

The quantity estimated is the percentage change in issue completion time due to AI, S = E[completion time with AI allowed] / E[completion time with AI disallowed] − 1; −50% would mean AI-allowed issues take half the time, 100% twice as long (§2.3, p. 6) [AE]. The authors usually report its absolute value and call negative values speedup and positive values slowdown, which they flag as "a mild abuse of language" [V], because speedup and slowdown are rates while the estimated quantity is a percentage change in time (§2.3, p. 6, footnote 8) [AR]. The outcome is total self-reported implementation time, pre- and post-review; for the small number of issues not reviewed or merged, post-review time is imputed with the condition's mean (§2.3, p. 6) [AE].

S is estimated with a log-linear OLS regression of log completion time on the treatment flag and the log of the developer's pre-randomization no-AI forecast (App. D.1, p. 28) [AE]. The forecast is included because it proxies difficulty and is highly predictive of completion time, raising statistical power without bias, since it was elicited before assignment (App. D.1, p. 28) [AR]. Developer fixed effects are generally left out because they explain minimal variation conditional on forecasts (App. D.1, p. 28, footnote 17) [AR]. Default intervals are 95% with HC3 standard errors; developer-clustered and bias-corrected cluster-robust (CR2, CR3) errors give similar results, and a hierarchical bootstrap resampling developers and then issues gives somewhat wider intervals (App. D.2, p. 28; Figure 15, p. 29) [AE]. Developer-level clustering is not necessarily recommended, following Abadie et al., because developer sampling is non-random and treatment is assigned per issue; it is appropriate if developer sampling is treated as random (App. D.2, p. 28, footnote 18) [BT]. Subgroup effects use interaction terms (App. D.4, p. 30) [AE]; a ratio-of-means estimator with pooled-bootstrap intervals is the robustness check and is also used for the aggregate change implied by developer forecasts (App. D.5, pp. 30–31) [AE]; post-study estimates are an issue-weighted mean of each developer's reported ratio (App. D.6, p. 31) [AE].

The authors convert the treatment coefficient β to percentage change in completion time with S = exp(β) − 1, where exp(β) equals the ratio of conditional mean completion times with and without AI (App. D.3, p. 29) [AP]. That equality holds provided the disturbance εᵢ is independent of both treatment status and the no-AI forecast and E[exp(εᵢ)] exists, since the common factor E[exp(εᵢ)] cancels in the ratio (App. D.3, p. 30, footnote 19) [AP]. Under standard regularity assumptions, which they say their diagnostics suggest hold, they build the 95% interval for β in the usual way and get the interval for S by applying exp(β) − 1 to its endpoints, S being a monotonic function of β (App. D.3, p. 30) [AP].

### Supplementary data (§2.4, pp. 7–8)

- *Developer forecasts and post hoc estimates*, collected before randomization and after the study (§2.4, p. 7) [AE].
- *Expert forecasts* from machine-learning experts (industry professionals from frontier AI labs and academics from universities with leading computer-science graduate programmes) and economics experts (mainly academics and PhD students), given detailed study information and paid by the rule max(0, $50 × (1 − (true answer − guessed answer)²)); about one-third were offered a $100 maximum (§2.4, p. 7, footnote 10) [AE]. The authors note that taking a maximum with 0 makes the scoring rule improper, citing Gneiting and Raftery, and use it for simplicity and clarity (§2.4, p. 7, footnote 11) [BT]. Experts predicted the ratio of no-AI to AI-allowed time, which the paper transforms for Figure 1; the authors note a forecaster's belief about one ratio need not be the reciprocal of their belief about the other (§2.4, p. 7, footnote 9; App. E.5, p. 34) [AR].
- *Cursor analytics* for the 13 developers given subscriptions: most-used model, and suggested and accepted lines of AI code (§2.4, p. 7) [AE].
- *Exit interviews and surveys* on where AI helped, elicitation strategies, perceived improvement, and estimated speedup (§2.4, p. 7) [AE].
- *Qualitative evidence* from developers' notes, clustered by inductive coding; because developers were also asked probing questions to test initial hypotheses, "so we cannot rule out bias from this type of qualitative evidence" [V] (§2.4, p. 7).
- *Screen-recording labels*: 128 recordings (143 hours) labelled at about 10-second resolution with high-level activity labels (writing code, testing and debugging, reading or searching, Git or environment, prompting AI, waiting on AI, reviewing AI outputs, idle or other) broken into 27 fine-grained categories; after removing issues with cheating, broken recordings (>10% of time) or a >20% gap between self-reported and recorded time, 74 recordings (84 hours) remain (§2.4, p. 8) [AE]. The 143 hours represent 29% of developers' total hours (§1, p. 2) [AE]. Shorter recordings were labelled first, and many developers did not record small post-review changes; "These factors may bias estimates of time allocation." [V] (App. G.8, p. 45).

## Part III: Results

### The slowdown (§3, p. 8)

Developers complete 136 AI-allowed and 110 AI-disallowed issues (§3, p. 8) [AE]. With AI allowed they take 19% more time on average, and nearly all quantiles of implementation time show AI-allowed issues taking longer (§3, p. 8; Figure 5, p. 9) [AE]: "That is, developers are slower when using AI is allowed." [V] (§3, p. 8). Read from Figure 1 (approximate, measured from a page render; the text states no value), the confidence interval for the observed change runs from about +1% to about +39% (Figure 1, p. 2) [AE]; the caption points to Appendix D for the confidence-interval methodology and does not state the interval's level (Figure 1, p. 2). The raw difference in average times is 34%, larger than the regression's 19% because AI-allowed issues ended up slightly more difficult by their AI-disallowed forecasts (not statistically significant), which the regression adjusts for and the ratio does not (§3.1, p. 9, footnote 12) [AE] [AR].

### Forecasts and calibration (§3.1, pp. 8–9; App. E.2, pp. 31–33)

Before each issue developers forecast a 24% speedup; after the study they estimate they were sped up by 20%, despite being slowed by 19% (§3.1, pp. 8–9) [AE]. Their forecasts still predict completion time: the Pearson correlation between forecast and actual time is 0.64 for AI-allowed issues and 0.59 for AI-disallowed ones, which the authors read as developers being "broadly well-calibrated on the relative amount of time that issues will take, but their expectations regarding the usefulness of AI assistance are reversed" [V] (§3.1, p. 9). 34 economics experts and 54 machine-learning experts predict decreases of 39% and 38%, overestimating speedup more than developers (§3.1, p. 9) [AE].

Per developer, 75% experience slowdown (App. E.2, p. 32) [AE]. Developers are also calibrated in a relative way: on issues where they forecast significant speedup (at least 33%, the top tertile), they are not slowed down, and slowdown decreases monotonically as forecasted speedup increases (App. E.2, p. 32; Figure 18, p. 33) [AE].

### How time is spent (§3.2, pp. 9–10)

On 74 issues with valid recordings, when AI is allowed developers spend a smaller share of time actively coding and reading or searching for information, and instead spend time reviewing AI outputs, prompting AI and waiting for generations; they also spend a somewhat higher share idle, with no activity on screen (§3.2, p. 9; Figure 6, p. 10) [AE].

## Part IV: The 21-factor analysis (§3.3, pp. 10–11; App. C, pp. 18–28)

The authors group 21 candidate factors into four categories: direct productivity loss (mechanisms by which AI use actively slows development), experimental artifact (confounders from setup or procedure that may bias results or limit external validity), factors raising developer performance relative to AI, and factors limiting AI performance relative to developers (§3.3, p. 10) [AP]. Using surveys, recordings, interviews and subset analyses, they find evidence that 5 contribute, mixed, unclear or no evidence for 10, and evidence against 6 (§3.3, p. 10) [AE]. They "strongly caution against over-indexing on the basis of any individual pieces of evidence, as we are not powered for statistically significant multiple comparisons when subsetting our data" [V], and describe the analysis as "speculative, suggestive evidence about the mechanisms behind slowdown" [V] (§3.3, p. 10).

### Factors likely to contribute (App. C.1, pp. 18–20)

**Over-optimism about AI usefulness (C.1.1; direct productivity loss).** Developers were told to use AI as much or as little as they found helpful, so one might expect the change in time to be bounded at 0%, since a developer seeing AI slow them down would stop using it (App. C.1.1, p. 18) [AR]. But developers hold an overoptimistic picture before and after (24% and 20%): "This overoptimistic view may lead developers to overuse AI assistance, despite its negative effect on their productivity." [V] (App. C.1.1, p. 18).

**High developer familiarity with repositories (C.1.2; raises developer performance).** Developers rated each issue's Prior Task Exposure (1–5) and External Resource Needs (1–3) before randomization, with cutoffs chosen for roughly balanced groups; these were collected only for the latter half of issues (App. C.1.2, pp. 18–19; Figure 7, p. 19) [AE]. Figure 7 gives moderate evidence that developers are slowed down more on issues where they have high prior exposure and where they need fewer external resources (App. C.1.2, p. 18) [AE]. Developers say AI helps more on unfamiliar work, such as unfamiliar datasets, a first frontend test, or first-time Git hooks (App. C.1.2, p. 19) [AE]. The authors add: "Sometimes, portions of one’s own codebase can be as unknown as a new API." [V] (App. C.1.2, p. 19). Where they are expert it helps much less; one developer says "if I am the dedicated maintainer of a very specialized part of the codebase, there is no way agent mode can do better than me." [V] (App. C.1.2, p. 19). The authors hypothesize that AI helps their developers less than in earlier studies [10; 11] because of their much greater repository experience, consistent with familiarity effects in Noy and Zhang and in Cui et al. (App. C.1.2, p. 19) [AR] [BT].

**Large and complex repositories (C.1.3; limits AI performance).** Developers report AI performing worse in complex environments: making unwanted changes in other parts of the code, and edit failures one developer tied to the size of the file being edited (App. C.1.3, p. 19) [AE]. The authors hypothesize that AI helps less than in earlier RCTs because the repositories average about 10 years old and over 1,100,000 lines of code, against the more greenfield projects in Peng et al., Paradis et al. and Weber et al., consistent with literature on environment complexity [3; 38; 39] (App. C.1.3, p. 19) [AR] [BT].

**Low AI reliability (C.1.4; limits AI performance).** Developers accept under 44% of Cursor generations (excluding 3 developers who used their own subscriptions); rejected generations lead to re-prompting or reverting (App. C.1.4, p. 20, footnote 13) [AE]. Reviewing, testing or modifying code before rejecting it wastes time; one developer "wasted at least an hour first trying to [solve a specific issue] with AI" [V] before reverting and implementing it without AI (App. C.1.4, p. 20). Even accepted code needs work: 75% report reading every line of AI code, 56% often make major changes to clean it up, and 100% report needing to modify it; one developer cites "more to fix up, in terms of code conventions, code style" [V] (App. C.1.4, p. 20). On 44 issues with valid labelled recordings, developers spend about 9% of AI-allowed time reviewing and cleaning AI outputs (App. C.1.4, p. 20) [AE].

**Implicit repository context (C.1.5; limits AI performance, raises developer performance).** Developers rely on undocumented knowledge of the codebase, which AI lacks; one says AI acts like a new contributor and "AI doesn’t pick the right location to make the edits." [V]; another that the model does not know the data: "It doesn’t know we need to take care of this weird case of backwards compatibility" [V] (App. C.1.5, p. 20). The authors hypothesize that repository size and maturity increase the tacit knowledge experienced developers rely on, which AI may lack access to (App. C.1.5, p. 20) [AR].

### Factors with an unclear effect (App. C.2, pp. 20–25)

- **Experimentally driven overuse of AI (C.2.1; artifact).** The study is not blinded. Developers' post-study self-descriptions ("using AI as normal", "experimenting with AI", "using as much AI as possible") do not show a clear effect in the text's reading of Figure 8, while the figure's caption says those experimenting or using AI as much as possible see greater slowdown than those using it as normal; several developers said participation sometimes led them to overuse AI unproductively (App. C.2.1, pp. 20–21) [AE].
- **Unrepresentative task distribution (C.2.2; artifact).** Developers called the issues entirely standard, and manual review confirms normal work, but issues were smaller than usual: "It was the same set of tasks, but sampled from the small end." [V] (App. C.2.2, pp. 20–21). Issue work excludes PR review and design discussion; selection may have made issues better scoped, which literature suggests helps AI but may help these experts too, "so the net effect of this selection is unclear" [V] (App. C.2.2, p. 21).
- **AI increasing issue scope (C.2.3; artifact).** Developers who report scope creep on AI-allowed issues are slowed down less, evidence against scope as the cause, though "it relies on developer self-reports of scope creep, which may be unreliable or subjective" [V] (App. C.2.3, p. 21). Reports are mixed: one developer says "AI was much more suggestable than I was." [V] (App. C.2.3, p. 21); others say AI led them to do more (App. C.2.3, pp. 21–22) [AE]. Developers write 47% more code per hour of AI-disallowed forecast on AI-allowed issues (p = 0.16, not significant), and lines of code need not mean more scope or productivity (App. C.2.3, p. 22) [AE] [AR].
- **Bias from issue completion order (C.2.4; artifact).** Developers choose the order after randomization; no one reported prioritizing by condition, but the authors lack access to developers' entire workflows, "so we cannot fully rule out this effect" [V] (App. C.2.4, p. 22).
- **Sampling bias in recruitment (C.2.5; artifact).** Developers who rely heavily on AI may have been less likely to join, not wanting to lose AI on 50% of tasks; this never came up in recruitment, but one developer later said they were unlikely to join a future iteration for that reason (App. C.2.5, p. 22, footnote 14) [AE] [AR].
- **Trading speed for ease (C.2.6; direct productivity loss).** Reports on effort are mixed: AI "felt like less effort." [V]; one developer "didn’t really think about some of the problems" [V]; another reported "no effort or approach difference [with AI]." [V] (App. C.2.6, p. 23). 69% of developers continue using Cursor after the study, and "This impressive retention rate suggests that developers are getting some significant value from using Cursor, and it seems unlikely this is solely a result of miscalibration on their productivity." [V] (App. C.2.6, p. 23).
- **Low quality initial pull requests (C.2.7; direct productivity loss).** Mean post-review time differs insignificantly (9 and 15 minutes for AI-disallowed and AI-allowed), and qualitatively AI-allowed PRs do not appear to be lower quality; 100% of developers report they "only submit high quality PRs" [V] (App. C.2.7, p. 23; App. C.3.4, p. 27).
- **Below-average use of AI tools (C.2.8; limits AI performance).** The authors see no meaningful difference by prior experience with Cursor, Copilot or web LLMs (Figure 10), and excluding up to each developer's first eight AI-allowed issues changes little (Figure 11), evidence against slowdown from missing basic skills that could be learned quickly (App. C.2.8, pp. 23–24) [AE]. Up to 50 hours of Cursor experience, more experience does not broadly reduce slowdown; the one developer with more than 50 hours shows positive speedup, so "it’s plausible that there is a high skill ceiling for using Cursor, such that developers with significant experience see positive speedup" [V] (App. C.2.8, p. 24). After publication a second developer corrected their prior Cursor experience to over 100 hours; they showed slowdown, and counting them would move the over-50-hours bucket's estimate from roughly 25% speedup to roughly 0%; the figure is left as-is for methodological consistency (App. C.2.8, p. 24, footnote 15) [AE]. Skills without AI may also atrophy, so observed speedup could come from weaker AI-disallowed work (App. C.2.8, p. 25) [AR]: "Overall, it’s unclear how to interpret these results, and more research is needed to understand the impact of learning effects with AI tools on developer productivity." [V] (App. C.2.8, p. 25). Developers use Cursor at a level comparable to the authors: "While we don’t expect that developers are using AI assistance optimally, we do not find evidence that they are below-average in AI tool use ability." [V] (App. C.2.8, p. 25).
- **AI generation latency (C.2.9; limits AI performance).** A minority report significant waiting; on the 44 labelled AI-allowed recordings developers spend about 4% of time waiting, small but non-trivial; there are likely fundamental tradeoffs between latency and performance or reliability, with the optimal point plausibly depending on the domain and on how humans use AI to substitute for their labour (App. C.2.9, p. 25) [AE] [AR].
- **Suboptimal elicitation (C.2.10; limits AI performance).** Developers use Cursor agent/composer and chat in 55% and 48% of AI-allowed issues, but normal use does not typically sample more than a few thousand tokens; limited token spend would not explain the gap with studies finding speedup [10; 17]; strategies such as sampling many agent trajectories and filtering with an LLM judge or self-consistency were not tested, so "it remains unclear how much effect these strategies would have on developer productivity in the wild" [V] (App. C.2.10, p. 25) [BT].

### Factors unlikely to contribute (App. C.3, pp. 25–28)

- **Unfamiliar development environment (C.3.1).** Restricting to developers using comparable IDEs in both conditions still gives a 24% slowdown, and Figure 12 shows no meaningful learning effect over the first 50 hours of Cursor use (App. C.3.1, p. 26) [AE].
- **Cheating or under-use of AI (C.3.2).** Developers use no AI in 16.4% of 44 labelled AI-allowed recordings; AI was used on 3 of 54 labelled AI-disallowed recordings (about 6%), and "At least one instance of observed cheating appears to be accidental." [V] (App. C.3.2, p. 26).
- **Issue dropout (C.3.3).** 3 developers leave 7 AI-disallowed issues uncompleted and 4 leave 6 AI-allowed ones; restricted subsets show slowdowns of 42%, 21% and 21%; 24 issues were dropped on purpose (leading reasons: 11 too hard, 5 no longer relevant, 3 done by another developer), and developers and manual review confirm none for reasons tied to condition (App. C.3.3, p. 26) [AE].
- **Non-robust outcome measure (C.3.4).** Imputed post-review times cover about 12% of issues (27), balanced across conditions; imputing an extreme one-hour bias for either condition gives 14% and 23% slowdowns; total screen-recording time gives 25% slowdown against 24% from self-reports on the same subset (App. C.3.4, p. 27) [AE].
- **Non-robust estimator (C.3.5).** A simple ratio estimator and three alternative regressions all give similar results (App. C.3.5, p. 27; Figure 13) [AE].
- **Non-frontier model usage (C.3.6).** In 44 labelled AI-allowed videos developers use Claude 3.7 Sonnet (thinking mode) 25%, Claude 3.7 Sonnet 34%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 23%, GPT-4o 11%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 3% and o1 2%, and no model 16.4%, excluding autocomplete; most issues were completed in February and March 2025, before models like Claude 4 Opus or Gemini 2.5 Pro were released (App. C.3.6, p. 28) [AE].

## Part V: Caveats and what the result does not show

### Key caveats (§4.1, p. 12)

"We caution readers against overgeneralizing on the basis of our results." [V] (§4.1, p. 12). High familiarity with the repositories and their size and maturity contribute to the slowdown and do not apply in many settings; "our results are consistent with small greenfield projects or development in unfamiliar codebases seeing substantial speedup from AI assistance" [V] (§4.1, p. 12). The authors expect that AI with higher reliability, lower latency, or better elicitation (more inference compute, more skilled prompting or scaffolding, fine-tuning on the repositories) could speed up developers in this setting (§4.1, p. 12) [AR]. Preliminary, forthcoming evidence suggests fully autonomous agents using Claude 3.7 Sonnet can often implement the core functionality of issues in several study repositories, though they "fail to fully satisfy all requirements" [V], typically omitting documentation, failing linting or styling rules, and leaving out key tests (§4.1, p. 12). "This represents immense progress relative to the state of AI just 1-2 years ago" [V], and if progress continues, which they call a priori at least plausible but not guaranteed, significant speedup may soon follow in this setting (§4.1, p. 12) [AR].

### Implications stated (§4, pp. 10–12)

"This observed slowdown serves as some evidence that AI capabilities in the wild may be lower than results on commonly used benchmarks may suggest." [V] (§4, p. 10). The over-estimation by experts and developers underscores "the importance of conducting field experiments with robust outcome measures, compared to relying solely on expert forecasts or developer surveys" [V] (§4, pp. 10–12).

### Potential misreadings (App. B, Table 2, p. 17)

The authors list claims the study does not support, each with a clarification (App. B, p. 17) [AR]:
- that AI does not currently speed up many or most developers: "We do not claim that our developers or repositories represent a majority or plurality of software development work" [V];
- that AI does not speed up people outside software development: "We only study software development" [V];
- that near-future AI will not speed up developers in this exact setting: "Progress is difficult to predict" [V], with substantial progress over the past five years;
- that there are no ways to use existing AI more effectively here: Cursor samples few tokens, may not prompt or scaffold optimally, and repository-specific training or few-shot learning could yield speedup;
- that developers with much more AI experience would not see speedup: plausibly much more experience could;
- that these developers are not sped up on any task: some developers are estimated to experience speedup (Figure 17).

## Part VI: Procedures and instruments (App. E–G)

### Randomization and balance (App. E.1, E.3, pp. 31–33)

Forecasted times do not differ meaningfully between conditions (Welch t-test p-values 0.28 and 0.56), which the authors read as successful randomization (App. E.1, p. 31; Table 4) [AE]. Assignment was 55.3% AI-allowed and 44.7% AI-disallowed against an intended 50/50 (chi-square p = 0.10, not significant) (App. E.1, p. 31; Table 5) [AE]. 25 early issues used a block randomization scheme that proved unworkable with small issue lists; excluding them still gives 20% slowdown, so they are kept for statistical power (App. E.3, p. 33; §2.2, p. 5, footnote 5) [AE].

### Activity breakdowns (App. E.4, pp. 33–34)

Appendix E.4 presents breakdowns of developers' time across activities: average minutes on high-level activities with AI allowed and disallowed (Figure 19, p. 33), average minutes across 27 fine-grained activity categories (Figure 20, p. 34), and the percentage of time on fine-grained activities with AI allowed and disallowed (Figure 21, p. 34) (App. E.4, pp. 33–34) [AP].

### Other treatment effects (App. E.6, pp. 34–35)

Appendix E.6 presents estimates using alternative outcome measures or subsets of the data, including a subset that excludes the 25 block-randomized issues (Figure 22, p. 35), and treatment effects by the calendar month in which issue implementation started, measured by first commit (Figure 23, p. 35) (App. E.6, pp. 34–35) [AP].

### Recruitment and incentives (App. G, G.1, G.6, pp. 37, 45)

Developers are recruited to select active contributors to repositories with more than 500 stars, through professional networks, Reddit's r/Python and r/MachineLearning, and GitHub profiles found from the 250 most popular repositories plus those tagged ai, llm, deep-learning and neural-networks, excluding contributors with fewer than five commits in the previous three months (App. G, p. 37) [AE]. 51 developers filled out a preliminary interest survey, about 20 were kept, and several dropped out early for reasons unrelated to the study (App. G, p. 37) [AE]. Data collection stopped for three more developers: two because their repository paused development indefinitely, one for widespread cheating in the first issues; all were paid in full and their issues are excluded (App. G.6, p. 45) [AE]. Pay is $150/hour with under five hours of study overhead; a per-issue bonus was rejected because it could lead developers to split issues or lower quality standards, and "We expect that paying developers per hour overall has minimal effect on their behavior, beyond encouraging them to participate in the study." [V] (App. G.1, p. 37).

### Developer instructions (App. G.2.1, pp. 37–42)

The recruitment document asks for at least 1 year of professional experience, at least 6 months as an active maintainer, and an open-source repository with at least 500 stars (or manual review as high-quality and mature) and at least 3,000 human-written lines of code, plus a list of improvement projects (App. G.2.1, pp. 37–38) [AE]. It asks for a minimum of 20 hours, caps funded hours around 40, and describes a 1–2 month pilot; it said task order would be slightly randomized, with a bracketed note in the paper that this was not done and was clarified with developers (App. G.2.1, p. 38) [AE]. Its stated motivation: to learn if or when AI could reshape software engineering, in particular when models might greatly speed up AI R&D and create a feedback loop accelerating AI progress; and because benchmarks fail to measure how much models speed up engineers in their real workflow, are artificial, need agent scaffolding that can get stuck, and saturate quickly (App. G.2.1, pp. 38–39) [AR]. Each issue carries a description, a label (bug fix, new feature, exploration, refactor), two time estimates (without AI, and with AI used to the best of the developer's ability), and ratings of Prior Task Exposure (1–5) and External Resource Needs (1–3); issues should ideally be under 4 hours, at most 2 if possible, with at least 10 issues and 20–40 hours in all (App. G.2.1, pp. 39–40) [AE]. During work developers record which models they use, link the PR and the Loom screen recording, track active initial and post-review implementation time separately, and rate perceived effort from 1 (minimal) to 5 (maximum) (App. G.2.1, pp. 40–42) [AE].

### Onboarding, check-ins and exit (App. G.3–G.5, pp. 42–45)

A 30-minute onboarding call trains developers in Cursor agent mode to the point of creating an agent instance, adding a file to its context, prompting a change, accepting it and reverting it (App. G.3, p. 42) [AE]. All developers were offered periodic 15-minute check-in calls, most had between 1 and 4, and the calls were also used to ask about their AI experience; developers also got periodic feedback on their notes and recordings, and occasional emailed tips such as reminders to tag relevant files when prompting agents (App. G.4, pp. 42–43; App. G, p. 37) [AE]. The exit interview (30 minutes to an hour, held 1 day to about 6 weeks after the last issue) was unstructured, following an outline that covered, among other topics, task selection, effort and focus, AI code cleaning, scope creep, future use, AI skill, waiting and idle time, and perceived effect (App. G.5, pp. 42–44) [AE]. The exit survey asks prior hours with LLMs and Cursor, end-of-study Cursor skill, repository quality practices, a speedup factor (2 for twice as fast, 0.5 for twice as slow), and how developers read and edit AI code (App. G.5.1, pp. 44–45) [AE].

### Screen-recording labels (App. G.8, pp. 45–50)

Labellers who program well and have used Cursor Composer label each stretch of a Loom video (reading the issue, writing or reading code, docs, tests, debugging, compiling, setup, Git operations, thinking, unrelated, paused, communicating) and the AI flow (writing a prompt, waiting on generation, reading a generation, generation taken or rejected, AI code cleaning), plus what the AI was used for and which model and interface; 1 in 10 submissions is checked and accurate labellers get a $250 bonus (App. G.8, pp. 46–50) [AE].

### Expert forecaster brief (App. G.9, pp. 50–51)

Experts received a description of open-source development, AI tooling, recruitment, issues, participation and the estimator, written while the study was part-way through; it asked them to predict the speedup factor S = mean(no-AI time) / mean(AI-allowed time) (App. G.9, pp. 50–51) [AE]. It gives 50 survey respondents, 31 introductory calls and 16 developers, 94% of whom had used web-based LLMs in development; its rates of prior VS Code, Copilot and Cursor use (63%, 56%, 25%) carry a bracketed note that they were preliminary and lower than the values reported in the paper (App. G.9, pp. 50–51) [AE].

### Primers (App. F, pp. 35–37)

The open-source primer defines repository, contributor, issue, pull request, review, merge, stars and forks, using pandas as the running example (45,200 stars, 18,400 forks) and noting that practice varies across projects (App. F.1, pp. 35–36) [AP]. The AI-tooling primer describes web chat interfaces and the models available in the study period, and Cursor as a fork of VS Code with chat and agent mode (an LLM that can explore the codebase, run commands and edit files, with changes shown for acceptance or rejection) and LLM-based autocomplete (App. F.2, pp. 36–37) [AP].

## Connections the author makes in the text

- Peng et al. (GitHub Copilot study), Paradis et al. (enterprise RCT), Weber et al.: speedups on synthetic or artificial tasks; cited as prior findings, with Peng et al.'s task criticised as unrepresentative of most software development work and likely to be similar to a large amount of LLM training data, which may unfairly advantage AI systems relative to humans [BT] (§1.1, p. 3; App. B, Table 3, p. 18; App. C.1.3, p. 19).
- Gambacorta et al., Yeverechyahu et al., Cui et al.: in-the-wild studies with output measures not fixed in advance [BT] (§1.1, p. 3; Table 3, p. 18); Cui et al. and Noy and Zhang cited as consistent with familiarity effects [BT] (App. C.1.2, p. 19).
- Agrawal, Gans and Goldfarb: AI as a fall in the cost of prediction [BT] (§1.1, p. 3).
- Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond; Noy and Zhang; Choi and Schwarcz: generative AI benefiting less experienced workers more; Brynjolfsson et al. and Noy and Zhang also cited for productivity gains outside software [BT] (§1.1, p. 3).
- Benchmark literature (RE-Bench, MLE-bench, PaperBench, CodeElo, SWE-Lancer, GPQA, HCAST) for frontier capabilities on software benchmarks, and Raji et al., Biderman et al. and Davis for lab tasks being self-contained and scored by metrics that miss important capabilities [BT] (§1, p. 1); SWE-bench and Liu et al. ("Lost in the middle") with RE-Bench on environment complexity [BT] (App. C.1.3, p. 19).
- Kwa et al. on the pace of AI progress [BT] (§1, p. 3; App. B, p. 17); the AI Index Report 2025 [BT] (§1, p. 1).
- CBRN uplift studies (Anthropic, RAND, Llama 3, OpenAI) with mixed results [BT] (§1.1, p. 3).
- Leibowich et al. on AI accelerating AI R&D; Erdil and Besiroglu, Erdil et al., Davidson on explosive growth; Acemoglu, Agrawal et al., Furman and Seamans on AI's economic impact [BT] (§1.1, p. 4).
- DellaVigna, Otis and Vivalt on forecasting experiment results [BT] (§2.4, p. 7); Gneiting and Raftery on proper scoring rules [BT] (§2.4, p. 7).
- Snell et al. on test-time compute; Wang et al. on self-consistency [BT] (App. C.2.10, p. 25).
- Abadie et al. on clustering; Cameron and Miller and Bell and McCaffrey on cluster-robust errors [BT] (App. D.2, p. 28; Figure 15, p. 29).
- Stack Overflow 2024 developer survey for VS Code as the most popular editor [BT] (App. F.2.2, p. 36).

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Inferring real-world impact from lab experiments on synthetic tasks.* They "sacrifice realism for scale and efficiency" and make inference to practice difficult (§1, p. 1; §1.1, p. 3).
- *Outcome measures not fixed in advance* (lines of code, commits, pull requests), which AI can move without productivity rising (§1, p. 1; §1.1, p. 3).
- *Relying solely on expert forecasts or developer surveys* in place of field experiments with robust outcome measures (§4, p. 12).
- *Benchmarks as a measure of how much models speed up engineers in real workflows* (App. G.2.1, pp. 38–39; §4, p. 10).
- *Over-generalising this study's result*, as listed in Table 2 (App. B, p. 17; §4.1, p. 12).
- *Paying bonuses per completed issue*, rejected because it could bias results (App. G.1, p. 37).

## Acknowledgments (§5, p. 12)

The authors thank the participating open-source developers; reviewers who gave feedback on the experimental design and paper drafts; and people who helped with data collection, technical support, operational support, graphic design, and close review, feedback and support throughout the project (§5, p. 12) [AP].

## Citation and source-integrity notes

**Conversion.** The original is the arXiv v2 PDF (51 pages, letter size; PDF metadata creator "arXiv GenPDF (tex2pdf:)"), at `sources/original/becker-metr-ai-developer-productivity-2025.pdf`, sha256 `3e18d9e097a3163dbae662e8b7c68ace0510be433891994b136ae7730beab25c`, fetched 2026-10-11 from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.09089v2. The tape (2,951 lines, 22,918 words) was made with `pdftotext` (poppler 26.08.0) in default reading-order mode, one page at a time, with a `{page-N}` marker before each page. Post-conversion check: 51 markers; folios 2–51 present and matching N; the end of G.9 is present; no truncation marker.

**Page anchors.** Page 1 prints no folio (confirmed against `pdftotext -layout` of p. 1); the "1" at tape line 29 is the Introduction's section number. Pages 2–51 print folios equal to N. On p. 29 the folio sits before the equation numbers "(4)" and "(5)" in the tape.

**Conversion artefacts, not quoted.** Table 1's category icons come through as stray glyphs ("Ý", "e", "Æ", or nothing); the category of each factor is taken from the C-section headings, which name it in words. Equations in App. D and the fractions in §2.4 footnote 9 and App. E.5 are linearised and partly scrambled; their content is taken from the surrounding prose. Tables 3, 7 and 8 are linearised column by column. Footnote numbers are glued to words ("condition1", "LLMs2"), and some line-end hyphens were dropped in joining ("AIdisallowed", "finegrained", "nearidentical", "selfconsistency"); quotations here avoid those words.

**Spellings and counts as printed.** Typos in the source, not quoted: "on on issues" (p. 18), "do do" (p. 22), "comparible" (p. 26), "alterative" (p. 37), "programatically" (p. 22). Table 4 prints a difference of 9 between means of 116 and 106. App. G gives 51 interest-survey respondents and App. G.9, written mid-study, gives n = 50. §3.2 gives 74 issues with valid recordings; App. C uses 44 labelled AI-allowed recordings and 54 labelled AI-disallowed recordings; the text does not state how these counts relate.

**Figure value.** Only Figure 1 was read from a render (p. 2, pdftoppm at 110 and 300 dpi, whisker caps measured in pixels against the axis ticks). The observed result's interval (about +1% to +39%) and the developer forecast and estimate intervals are approximate; the text states none of them, and the caption gives no interval level (it points to Appendix D for the methodology), so this reference does not label them 95% intervals. No other figure-only value is recorded.

**Authors.** The byline and Appendix A give "Beth Barnes"; the PDF metadata and the paper's references [2], [3] and [9] give "Elizabeth Barnes". Becker and Rush are marked as equal contribution. Appendix A: Becker and Rush designed, implemented and led the project; Barnes gave feedback and guidance; Rein contributed substantially to the writing and framing.

**Licence and scope.** The PDF carries no licence statement; the licence `CC BY 4.0` is as the arXiv abstract page states it. Scope is `open`.

**Images.** Text-only for this run; Figures 1–23 are not classified here.

**What this reference does not carry.** No claims about the cited works beyond how the paper cites them; nothing about METR or the authors beyond what the paper states; no figure value other than those read from Figure 1. Pass I: see the stamp on line 2 and the audit log.
